title: Big Shot Pictures Appoints Adam Rosenberg as Head of Film
description:
Big Shot Pictures has announced movie executive and producer Adam Rosenberg as its new head of film. 

	Rosenberg will lead the family entertainment
body:
Big Shot Pictures has announced movie executive and producer Adam Rosenberg as its new head of film. 

	Rosenberg will lead the family entertainment company’s feature film development and production, leveraging its multi-year deal with Sony Pictures Entertainment. 

	“Adam is a dynamic creative force with a stellar track record of steering some of the most acclaimed franchises,” said Brian Robbins, the founder of Big Shot Pictures. “As we build a modern studio designed for how audiences connect with content today, Adam will bring invaluable studio experience and taste to our forward-thinking digital vision.”
	

	Rosenberg added, “Big Shot is making a great bet on beloved stories, bold new ones and meeting families where they actually are today. What Brian and the team have built in such a short time is remarkable and I’m thrilled to be joining them.”


	Before joining Big Shot Pictures, Rosenberg co-founded Modern Magic, where he produced the animated film “Goat” for Sony Pictures Animation. He previously served as co-president of production at MGM, working there for ten years. While there, he executive produced “Creed III” and oversaw production on films such as “Candyman,” “Respect” and “The Magnificent Seven.” Beginning his career as an assistant to Scott Rudin, Rosenberg also served as senior vice president at Spyglass. 

	Big Shot Pictures recently acquired the “Eloise” franchise earlier this year, as well as a $25 million stake in “Alvin and the Chipmunks” via a joint venture with Bagdasarian Productions. The entertainment company is also in pre-production for an anime series written and produced by “One Piece” showrunner Matt Owens.

schema.headline: Big Shot Pictures Appoints Adam Rosenberg as Head of Film

title: ‘Boys for Life’ Cast: Alex Wolff, Will Angus and More Almost Friday Stars to Lead Paramount Primal Comedy (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
“Boys for Life,” the R-rated comedy movie from Tyler Falbo, has set its ensemble cast.

	Alex Wolff, Will Angus, Billy Langdon, Liam Cullagh, Cheste
body:
“Boys for Life,” the R-rated comedy movie from Tyler Falbo, has set its ensemble cast.

	Alex Wolff, Will Angus, Billy Langdon, Liam Cullagh, Chester Collins and Eilise Patton will star in the Paramount Primal film, which, as Variety broke in July, will open theatrically on April 9, 2027.

	Plot details are being kept under wraps, but Variety hears “Boys for Life” is a comedy about a group of friends with a dark twist. The project entered production earlier this summer.
	

	Aside from Wolff, the cast consists of the comedic minds behind Almost Friday TV, a sketch crew born out of the digital media company Almost Friday Media. Falbo is the group’s de facto showrunner, producing high-concept videos for YouTube. He directs “Boys for Life” and co-wrote the film’s script with Almost Friday co-founder Max Barrett. Falbo also produces alongside Galen Core.

	Wolff, of “Naked Brothers Band” childhood fame, will soon be seen reprising his role in the fifth “Jumanji” movie, out Dec. 25. His credits also include the upcoming “Outside of Cleveland” as well as “Hereditary,” “Oppenheimer” and “Magic Farm.” He will soon star in his sophomore directorial effort, “If She Burns.”

	Angus broke out in the Mindy Kaling comedy show “Not Suitable for Work” and will next be seen in Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman movie “Artificial” alongside Andrew Garfield.

	Langdon, Cullagh and Collins are all founding members of Almost Friday TV, for which they write and act in viral comedy sketches. They also perform live comedy on tour. Alongside Patton, Angus and Falbo, they are developing a comedy series titled “Last Night Was a Movie” for FX.
	

	Under the Almost Friday umbrella, Collins is best known for his portrayal of the fictional alpha male entrepreneur Royce du Pont. Variety broke the news last year that Almost Friday is developing a mockumentary show around the character.

	In addition to her work at Almost Friday, Patton is a member of the esteemed Groundlings Main Company in Los Angeles. She appeared on ABC’s “The Rookie” and will lend her voice to the upcoming Netflix animated series “Dang.”

	Paramount Primal is the studio’s new genre label headed by J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, whose Boulderlight Pictures produced “Weapons,” “Friendship” and “Companion.” Paramount Primal aims to partner with both next-generation storytellers and established filmmakers to produce “smartly budgeted films” across horror, comedy, action and grounded sci-fi. The label recently acquired the U.S. rights to adapt the original screenplay for “A Nightmare on Elm Street” from the Wes Craven estate.

	Wolff is represented by Untitled Entertainment, WME and 2PM Sharp. Angus is repped by Mosaic, UTA and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern, LLP. Langdon is repped by Mosaic, UTA and Fox Rothschild. Cullagh is repped by Mosaic, UTA and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern, LLP. Collins is repped by Range, UTA and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern, LLP. Patton is repped by Brillstein Entertainment Partners, UTA and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

title: How ‘Pluribus’ Star Carlos Manuel Vesga Built Manousos’ Pilgrimage of Faith, Exile and Resistance
description: A game popular in Colombia, a person’s nationality, an icon of the Virgin Mary, spoken mantras — it’s details like these that gave Emmy-nominated “P
body: A game popular in Colombia, a person’s nationality, an icon of the Virgin Mary, spoken mantras — it’s details like these that gave Emmy-nominated “Pluribus” star Carlos Manuel Vesga the foundation on which to build his character, Manousos.Colombian star of TV, film and the stage, Vesga points out that Manousos is a Colombian immigrant living in Paraguay when the aliens join the entire world in one hive mind, aka “the joining,” and, like Carol (Rhea Seehorn), is one of 13 people in the world not joined. Also like Carol, Manousos is vehemently, almost violently, opposed to the hive mind — so much so that he rejects food and other comforts from them.“He has gone through the process of leaving his home country, severing his roots, leaving behind his old identity, and trying to build another one, in a foreign, unknown land,” Vesga says. “I think that explains and informs a lot on why he reacts the way that he does toward the joining — he’s someone who has lost before, and now he goes, ‘You know what? Not again!’”Manousos’ work ethic is also important to the character; it’s one that you see a lot in immigrants, he says.The production department also helped with the details, including a popular Colombian game called frog in the storage facility office.“They took the time and detail to build a frog game to put in Manus’ office, and they painted it with the Colombian flag,” Vesgas notes. “That’s how far they went. So when I walked on set, and I saw that, I can’t describe the feeling. I’m thousands of miles away from my home, and yet this makes me feel like I’m home.”Though Manousos has a small Virgin Mary symbol hanging from his car’s mirror, Vesga doesn’t think he is religious; Catholicism is just part of who he is.“I do think that this is a guy who can believe,” Vesga says. Manousos’ goal is to find Carol so they can save the world from the hive mind. “I think he has faith. In this case, he has faith in Carol. He totally believes that this woman out there in Albuquerque is the promised land, andhe trusts her so much that he goes through everything he goes through to get to Albuquerque.”His journey to Carol is more like a pilgrimage. The determined and hyper-focused Manousos teaches himself English; the beginner phrases become mantras.“I can imagine pilgrims in the Middle Ages reciting their mantras, repeating the rosary beads; it allows you to get into this trancelike state,” he says. Manousos keeps focus by repeating the beginner English phrases he is learning: “Monday is today, tomorrow will be Tuesday,” or “The yellow dog chases the gray cat” or “My name is Manousos Oviedo. I am not one of them. I wish to save the world.”The filming locations also helped inform Vesga’s journey. “It was hard not to feel the solitude in those places. It was really impossible not to feel small and alone, and yet, at the same time, feel the vastness of the world,” he says.Before Manousos embarks on the Darién Gap trail, the “others” come to warn him of its dangers, particularly the changa tree with its poisonous spikes. The production team researched the area, a treacherous pathway for immigrants trying to get to the U.S., creating a haunting start for Manousos. “They had used the images that they had researched from the Darién Gap, and how the trail is full of things that people leave behind,” Vesga says, noting the backpacks, clothes and, especially poignant, toys and children’s effects.It’s foreshadowing for what befalls him on the trail. Vesga recalls his scream for a scene in which he is impaled on the tree spikes: “We did it several times, and every time I would scream, my scream would echo through the whole place.”That echo underscores Manousos: he’s a loner, driven on a pilgrimage to save humanity.

schema.headline: How ‘Pluribus’ Star Carlos Manuel Vesga Built Manousos’ Pilgrimage of Faith, Exile and Resistance

title: American Film Market Expands With Launch of AFM House, Site of Its Innovation Hub
description: The American Film Market is expanding its scope with the launch of a new Los Angeles venue called The AFM House that will be site of its Innovation
body:
The American Film Market is expanding its scope with the launch of a new Los Angeles venue called The AFM House that will be site of its Innovation Hub.

	The Independent Film & Television Alliance (IFTA), that produces the AFM, on Wed, announced the new venue located across from the Fairmont Century Plaza. The AFM House adds 15,000 square feet of indoor and outdoor space to the market’s campus, “creating a dynamic gathering place for innovators, entrepreneurs, filmmakers, creators, cinema owners, distributors, investors and global brands to explore the ideas, technologies and business models shaping the future of the global screen economy,” IFTA said in a statement.
	

	The AFM House’s current centerpiece is the Innovation Hub, presented in collaboration with Cannes Next, the Marché du Film’s innovation program, launched in 2025. This year’s Hub will feature AI startups, leading tech companies, and forward-looking content. “The collaboration between the two markets underscores a shared commitment to championing innovation, fostering opportunities, and strengthening connections across the global film ecosystem,” according to the statement.


	Additionally, the AFM’s new venue will feature The Cinemas Club event co-created by the Marché du Film and Cine Group that comprises a speaker series focused on the future of theatrical cinema. Introduced at the Cannes 2026 Marché du Film. The Cinemas Club brings together cinema exhibitors, theatre owners, distributors, producers and industry experts “for curated discussions on the future of theatrical exhibition, audience engagement and the evolving cinema experience,” the statement noted.
	

	As previously announced, the 2026 American Film Market is set to take place at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles on Nov. 10–15.

	The AFM House will be open Nov. 11-14. The new venue will bring the market’s 2026 theme, “The New Global Screen Economy” to life “through fireside chats, presentations and networking, alongside a dedicated marketplace showcasing the people, companies, technologies and services transforming the business of film and television,” according to IFTA. 

	“Filmmaking has always been rooted in collaboration and innovation, and that spirit is more important today than ever,” IFTA president and CEO Jackie Brenneman said in the statement.

	“As our business continues to evolve at an unprecedented pace, The AFM House provides a place where the global entertainment community can come together to exchange ideas, forge partnerships, explore emerging business models and discover opportunities,” she added. “Our collaboration with Cannes Next and the Cinemas Club expand that vision by creating a dedicated home for innovation, technology, and the future of theatrical exhibition.” 

	Marché du Film executive director Guillaume Esmiol commented: “At the Marché du Film, we have built a growing portfolio of programs designed to address the major transformations shaping our industry, from AI and emerging technologies with Cannes Next to the future of theatrical exhibition through the Cinemas Club, co-created with Cine Group.” 

	“We are delighted to see these initiatives extend beyond Cannes through this expanded collaboration. AFM is creating an ambitious new platform with The AFM House, and we look forward to connecting companies and ideas, and creating new opportunities for the global film industry throughout the year,”  Esmiol continued.

	Julien Marcel, president of Cine Group, said: “After a strong first edition at the Marché du Film last May, we are delighted to bring the Cinemas Club to the AFM in Los Angeles. Theatrical exhibition has rarely needed more of what this market stands for: a broader and more diverse slate of films reaching screens, and the same appetite for innovation in the experience we offer audiences and in the way we connect with them.”

schema.headline: American Film Market Expands With Launch of AFM House, Site of Its Innovation Hub

title: Quest Marks, Former Bravo Marketer, Joins The Shop as VP, Creative
description: Quest Marks, a veteran marketing executive who had a hand in promoting some of Bravo‘s best-known programs, is joining The Shop, an entertainment-ma
body:
Quest Marks, a veteran marketing executive who had a hand in promoting some of Bravo‘s best-known programs, is joining The Shop, an entertainment-marketing boutique that helps devise trailers and promotional campaigns for some of the sector’s biggest venues.

	Marks will serve as vice president of creative, and will work across both TV and theatrical clients. He will also help build out The Shop’s social and digital capabilities.


	“The Shop absolutely loved working with Quest during his time at Bravo,” said Jordan Hayman, founder of The Shop, in a prepared statement.  “He’s an exceptional creative, so bringing Quest in was a no-brainer for us It provides us more senior leadership that’s imperative to our growth.”
	

	The company has in recent months helped devise promotional video for Apple TV’s “Down Cemetery Road”; Netflix’ “Love Is Blind”; Hulu’s “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives”; the return of “Scrubs” to Disney’s ABC; and Bravo’s “Below Deck.”

	Marks worked for 20 years at NBCUniversal, most recently as vice president of creative marketing at Bravo. As part of his remit, he worked closely with the network’s social team on creative for Bravo’s social video content while continuing to lead its on-air promotion strategy. He was previously senior creative director, on-air promotion at Bravo. During his time at the network, Marks worked on the award winning “Summer By Bravo” brand campaign and helped shape BravoCon and Bravo FanFest, the network’s fan convention properties. He recently led creative for the launch of “The Real Housewives of Rhode Island, “the newest entry in the “Real Housewives” franchise.
	

	“I’ve always enjoyed collaborating with The Shop on the client side, said Marks, who called the chance to join the company ” an opportunity I couldn’t resist.”

	Marks will report to partners Hayman and Nick Shakarian.

schema.headline: Quest Marks, Former Bravo Marketer, Joins The Shop as VP, Creative

title: ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Review: Wile E. Coyote Stars in a Courtroom Comedy That Blends Cartoons and Live Action. But the Fizz of Anarchy Is Missing
description: Hardly a day goes by without someone saying, in reference to an edgy piece of pop culture, “They could never make that today.” It almost seems as if
body:
Hardly a day goes by without someone saying, in reference to an edgy piece of pop culture, “They could never make that today.” It almost seems as if some people like saying that too much — as if they secretly approve of the fact. But in certain cases, there’s simply no denying the truth of it. If someone at Nickelodeon today, or the Disney Channel or the Cartoon Network, tried to program a series of animated shorts as violent and anarchic and demented and sadomasochistic as the Wile E. Coyote and Road Runner cartoons created and (mostly) directed by Chuck Jones, starting in 1949, that person might be called up on charges.
	

	That, of course, is exactly why those cartoons were impossibly great. To those of us who grew up on them, watching Wile E. Coyote do everything in his power to catch and kill the Road Runner gave off a charge of reckless endangerment that was hilarious and cathartic. It was also disarmingly casual. Every time Wile E. got blown to smithereens by a faulty detonator, or dropped 1,000 feet off a cliff to a distant puff-of-smoke crash landing, we experienced the comedy of pure aggression — and the comedy of ironic resilience. That Wile E. always bounced right back in the next scene lent the crazed destruction a weirdly optimistic undercurrent.


	“Coyote vs. Acme,” a studio comedy that combines famous cartoon characters and live action in the style of “Who Framed Roger Rabbit” (and also in the style of dozens of cheesy-bad franchise hybrids like the “Garfield” and “Alvin and the Chipmunks” and “Casper” and “Stuart Little” films), is a movie that wants to pay homage to the prankish exuberance of the “Looney Tunes” and “Merrie Melodies” cartoons. The movie is about how Wile E. Coyote, after too many years of failing to catch the Road Runner, mostly because every gizmo and dastardly piece of equipment he ever put toward the task (dynamite, anvils, magnetic gloves) failed to work, decides to sue the Acme Corporation, the manufacturer of each of those faulty products. Will Forte, wearing a beard and a flop of geek hair, is Kevin Avery, the late-night-TV-ad lawyer who takes the case.
	

	At heart, “Coyote vs. Acme” is a courtroom comedy. But the upshot of the movie is to integrate as much Road Runner-style mayhem as possible into a live-action universe. The film is chock-full of nods and references and jokey Looney Tunes Easter eggs. It could have been called “Remembrance of Rube Goldberg Bombs Past.”

	Yet there’s a certain way that “Coyote vs. Acme,” next to those cartoons, feels neutered and tame. The movie will serve up an escalating gag, like the Road Runner eating metal pellets so that Wile E. can trap him with a magnet, only to see Wile E. magnetized by a speeding train. But the staging doesn’t have the sustained, rollicking ferocity that made some of those cartoons as freewheeling in their maniacal slapstick as “Raiders of the Lost Ark.” “Coyote vs. Acme” keeps giving you the feeling that it’s referencing that earlier universe, rather than immersing you in it. That’s partly because the movie isn’t trying to be a live-action Road Runner cartoon, but also because it stops short of conjuring their insane spirit.

	The movie was inspired by Ian Frazier’s 1990 New Yorker story (a rather labored piece of whimsy), which treats Wile E. Coyote’s lawsuit against Acme with put-on bureaucratic seriousness. “Coyote vs. Acme,” however, is looser and lighter. It really does just want to be piece of nostalgic cartoon hijinks, and to that end it’s got a winning gregariousness. The film was scripted by Samy Burch, the gifted screenwriter of “May December” and “Late Fame,” and she does a meticulous job of orchestrating conspiracies and cartoon cameos. It’s all worked out on paper. Yet the film is missing something: the delirious fizz of true anarchic bedlam.

	Wile E. Coyote is our hero, and he’s his familiar wordless disgruntled self (though he holds up funny signs on occasion to indicate what he’s thinking). But we don’t see enough of the sneaky side of Wile E., the hungry predator who’s almost like the Grinch. Meanwhile, Will Forte gives a one-note performance as Avery, the lawyer who’s stuck in a mode of desperate high dudgeon. I’ve often felt allergic to animation-meets-live-action movies, because the live-action parts tend to get reduced to monotonous cartoons. That’s kind of what happens here. Forte’s frantic ambulance chaser, Lana Condor as his legal-assistant niece, John Cena as the grimacing Acme Corporation defense attorney — it’s all thin stuff.
	

	“Coyote vs. Acme” will play in theaters starting Aug. 28, but the movie has, of course, been through its own obstacle course. After being completed, it was shelved by its studio, Warner Bros. Pictures, only to become something of a cause célèbre among vintage cartoon fans. The movie certainly deserves to be released — and thanks to the independent distributor Ketchup Entertainment, which bought it from Warner Bros. for $50 million, that is now happening. But will the purchase prove to be worth it? “Coyote vs. Acme” would like to be a classic-cartoon version of “Roger Rabbit,” but I’m afraid it just plays like a polite and mildly likable look back at yesterday’s cartoon madness.

	The film’s most winning gambit it to sprinkle “Looney Tunes” and “Merrie Melodies” characters throughout the story. Tweety Bird is used nicely, as is Daffy Duck, who dominates the film’s explosive opening scene (getting trapped in goo during a top-secret Acme test film). But only two legendary characters truly get to throw their weight around — that grandiose Southern-fried sociopath Foghorn Leghorn, who’s the CEO of Acme, and the great Bugs Bunny, who is always wilier than anyone, including poor Wile E.

	As Wile. E. and the Roadrunner discover that they’re frenemies who need each other, the movie ends up taking a moral stand against the Acme Corporation. It’s revealed that there’s a sinister reason why the company’s products kept blowing up in Wile E.’s face. But who wants to see Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner turned into the dramatic linchpins of a Looney Tunes “Erin Brockovich”? It’s true that you couldn’t make Road Runner cartoons today. But you can make a movie like “Coyote vs. Acme,” which melts down anarchy into presentable buddy mishegas.

schema.headline: ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Review: Wile E. Coyote Stars in a Courtroom Comedy That Blends Cartoons and Live Action. But the Fizz of Anarchy Is Missing

title: Box Office: ‘End of Oak Street’ Targets $25 Million Debut, ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ to Remain No. 1
description:
Anne Hathaway, Ewan McGregor and a pack of rogue dinosaurs won’t be able to catch the web-slinging Spider-Man at the top of box office charts.

	Son
body:
Anne Hathaway, Ewan McGregor and a pack of rogue dinosaurs won’t be able to catch the web-slinging Spider-Man at the top of box office charts.

	Sony and Marvel’s comic book juggernaut “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is poised to dominate in North America during its third weekend of release. That’s despite five new nationwide releases: the Warner Bros. sci-fi mystery “The End of Oak Street” with Hathaway and McGregor, Paramount’s animated sequel “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie,” Black Bear’s crime thriller “The Rivals of Amziah King” starring Matthew McConaughey, Neon’s stoner comedy “The Wrong Girls” led by Kristen Stewart, the Angel Studios historical drama “The Brink of War.”
	

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” could earn another $65 million to $70 million over the weekend, a roughly 55% decline. After just 12 days on the big screen, the Tom Holland-led adventure is already the highest-grossing movie of the year with $671 million domestically and $1.68 billion globally. With breathless hype and repeat viewings galore, the superhero sequel will cross $2 billion worldwide at a near-record pace. It’s especially significant considering only seven films ever — “Avatar,” “Avengers: Endgame” and “Titanic” among them — have surpassed that benchmark during their theatrical runs. It’ll be Hollywood’s first $2 billion blockbuster since 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water.” 


	“The End of Oak Street” is targeting the biggest debut among newcomers, with projections ranging from $20 million to $30 million from 3,400 theaters. Warner Bros. is offering an estimate of $18 million to $23 million domestically, as well as $20 million to $25 million overseas. The movie carries a budget above $80 million, so positive word-of-mouth will be crucial to ensure that “Oak Street” remains a draw through August. David Robert Mitchell wrote and directed the PG-13 survival thriller, which follows a mysterious cosmic event that transports a suburban family to prehistoric times. “End of Oak Street” is the third big movie this summer to star Hathaway, who also leads “The Odyssey” and “The Devil Wears Prada 2.” And her year of box office domination will continue with October’s thriller “Verity.”
	

	Another primeval adventure of sorts, “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie” is aiming for $20 million from 3,500 North American theaters. Those estimates are similar to the prior “PAW Patrol” sequel, 2023’s “The Mighty Movie,” which ignited to $22 million and eventually climbed to $205 million globally against a $30 million budget. “The Dino Movie” carries a slightly larger $40 million price tag, which was split between Paramount and Spin Master.

	“The Dino Movie” launched last weekend at the international box office, where the kid-friendly movie has generated $27.5 million to date. Beyond the box office, “PAW Patrol” remains a consumer products juggernaut. The franchise, based on the popular Nickelodeon television series about rescue pups, has generated more than $14 billion in global retail sales since 2014. 

	“PAW Patrol” could benefit from pent-up demand since there hasn’t been a movie aimed at youngsters since “Minions & Monsters” in early July. With “The Dino Movie” catering to pre-schoolers and their parents, “The Wrong Girls,” “The Rivals of Amziah King” and “The Brink of War” are hoping to serve as counter-programming for older crowds. All three films are targeting single-digit debuts.

	“The Wrong Girls,” which opens in 510 locations, stars Stewart and Alia Shawkat as two codependent best friends who get caught up in a case of mistaken identity after getting high. Stewart’s wife Dylan Meyer wrote and directed the movie in her feature debut.

	The Rivals of Amziah King,” also landing on about 500 screens, follows McConaughey as a honeymaker and born-again Christian whose former foster daughter reappears in his life. It’s the sophomore feature from director Andrew Patterson. 

	“The Brink of War” is playing on 2,000 screens over the weekend. Set during the Reykjavík Summit of 1986, the movie stars Jeff Daniels as Ronald Reagan as he races against time to salvage a deal with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev (Jared Harris) to dismantle nuclear arsenals.

	Elsewhere, “The Odyssey” could add $17 million to $20 million in its fifth weekend on the big screen. Universal’s big-budget adaptation of Homer’s original epic has generated $466 million in North America and $1.11 billion globally. It’s the second-biggest movie of the year, following “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” as well as Christopher Nolan’s highest-grossing release of all time, ahead of 2012’s “The Dark Knight Rises” with $1.08 billion (not adjusted for inflation).
	

	Thanks to “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey” and other blockbusters, the summer box office has eclipsed $4 billion for just the second time since the pandemic. With a few weeks until Labor Day and a smattering of new releases to come, it’ll easily wind up as the biggest popcorn season since 2019.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘End of Oak Street’ Targets $25 Million Debut, ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ to Remain No. 1

title: ‘Don’t Say Good Luck’ Review: Sunny Sandler and Melanie Lynskey Give Genuine Soul to Netflix’s Mother-Daughter Heartbreaker
description: There’s a high probability that you’ve seen Sunny Sandler on screen before: Thanks to the patronage of her ceaselessly prolific dad, Adam, the 17-ye
body:
There’s a high probability that you’ve seen Sunny Sandler on screen before: Thanks to the patronage of her ceaselessly prolific dad, Adam, the 17-year-old has amassed 26 film credits to date. In “Don’t Say Good Luck,” however, you’ll actually notice her. As a teenager likewise stepping into the spotlight for the first time — and, in rather more bittersweet circumstances, facing the end of childhood — she’s the warmly gawky, thoroughly believable center of Julia Hart‘s sensitive, open-hearted theater-kid portrait. She’s matched beat for beat by Melanie Lynskey, no revelation but reliably affecting and emotionally generous as our heroine’s doting, ailing mother. Coming-of-age films with variations of these characters and dynamics come around pretty often; rather more unusual are those written and played with this degree of care and compassion.
	

	The latest collaboration between Netflix and Adam Sandler‘s Happy Madison Productions, “Don’t Say Good Luck” is markedly more delicate and deeply felt than most films bearing that imprint, though it’s still proudly mainstream in sensibility — unafraid of sentimentality as it lunges directly and most effectively for viewers’ heartstrings. Hart’s family-friendly “Stargirl” films for Disney+ showed she could balance mega-streamer house style with human-feeling storytelling; her more adventurous 2018 superhero indie “Fast Color” demonstrated a mature, cross-generational approach to frequently juvenile genre fare. 


	Those skills serve Hart well in her broadly empathetic latest, which should play relatably both to adolescents beginning to assert identities outside their parents’ control, as well as to elders grappling with a lifelong duty of care to their children and an obligation, sooner or later, to let go. For suburban mom-of-three Elizabeth (Lynskey), who balances childcare with a job running a popular local deli alongside her husband Ted (Max Greenfield), that may be too soon: Years after beating cancer, she’s dismayed to learn it has returned, this time with a tougher prognosis. 
	

	The script, co-written by Hart and producer/partner Jordan Horowitz with story scribe Laura Hankin, limns this crisis without any of the usual expository medical-consultation scenes; the focus throughout is intimately domestic, as Elizabeth reckons not just with her health but with how to alternately protect and prepare her family in the face of a worst-case scenario. Her boisterous pre-teen twins Ethan and Caleb are too young to grasp quite what’s at stake; high school sophomore Sophie (Sandler) has rather more vivid memories of going through this anguish before.

	But Sophie has a lot on her plate besides, beginning with the lead role in her school’s ambitious spring production of the Broadway musical “Waitress” — an unexpected coup over resident drama-club queen Mallory (an excellent Elyse Bell, bringing more nuance to this nascent-diva role than initially meets the eye), after her unassuming but purely sung audition strikes a chord with kindly teacher/director Ms. Parker (Stephanie Beatriz). It’s more work and pressure than she bargained for, putting strain on her relationship with longtime best friend Carolyn (Scarlett Estevez), who’s on her own path of queer self-discovery, and that’s before mounting family drama makes it increasingly hard for her to leave everything behind on stage.

	There’s a lot of room here for flat teen-movie stereotypes, but “Don’t Say Good Luck” — the title a running bit between Sophie and Elizabeth, who cherishes her daughter’s thespian dreams — is persistently, pleasingly fair to all involved, finding complicating seams of vulnerability in characters set up as foils or antagonists. Jack (Jack Champion), Sophie’s handsome co-lead and crush, is neither dreamboat nor dickhead, just a boy not yet in command of his various talents; Linda (Bebe Neuwirth), Elizabeth’s officious mother, may run a little cold, but controls what she can to counter life’s ungovernable cruelties. As family tensions build, her sweeter other half Dale, played with winningly soft squareness by Steve Buscemi, gives Sophie the plain, solid advice she needs: “You can let it out,” he counsels. “If not with me, then with somebody.”

	It’s a potentially corny line delivered with finely tuned gentleness, which goes for much else here. Lynskey, so good at playing weary, careworn decency, makes heart-to-heart dialogue sound, well, actually from the heart, rather than mawkishly platitudinous; Sandler returns her sincerity with a lovely performance that captures the needy, girlish terror and exploratory adult curiosity at play in her character. 
	

	Her vocals, bright and plaintive and without musical-theater affectation, are exactly as imperfect as they need to be, though Hart gifts her with a full, climactically blossoming musical sequence at exactly the right moment, singing the signature Sara Bareilles ballad “She Used to Be Mine” — at which point any misty-eyed viewers who have barely been hanging on up to this point will likely take Buscemi’s advice. Commendably thoughtful and quietly humane for much of its running time, “Don’t Say Good Luck” also knows just when to let it out.

schema.headline: ‘Don’t Say Good Luck’ Review: Sunny Sandler and Melanie Lynskey Give Genuine Soul to Netflix’s Mother-Daughter Heartbreaker

title: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Review: End-of-the-Summer Trash That’s Like a Loopier (and in Some Ways Better) ‘Jurassic’ Movie
description: “The End of Oak Street” belongs to the genre I call the last-gasp-of-summer movie. A movie in this category has several characteristics, starting wi
body:
“The End of Oak Street” belongs to the genre I call the last-gasp-of-summer movie. A movie in this category has several characteristics, starting with the fact that it has to be released in the middle of August or later. Beyond that, a last-gasp-of-summer movie is trashy and obvious, it’s usually ripped off from other movies, and it wears a shameless grin on its face about all of that. At the same time, it demands a certain size and scale — a straggling pretense of popcorn lavishness that marks it as a genuine final entry in the blockbuster season. (If it’s any smaller, you know that the summer is already over.)
	

	In “The End of Oak Street,” a tranquil middle-class neighborhood gets attacked by dinosaurs, so it wouldn’t be inaccurate to call the film “Jurassic World: Suburban Apocalypse.” There have been seven “Jurassic” movies, but to some of us it feels like there have been 27, and “The End of Oak Street” might as well be the 28th. The film has nothing whatsoever to do with that fabled franchise, but rarely have I encountered such a blatant piece of corporate cinematic piggybacking. Part of the joke is that the filmmakers are brazenly aware that today’s audiences couldn’t care less whether “The End of Oak Street” is an official “Jurassic” movie or not. The film seems to be saying: I’m a relentless, over-the-top junk dinosaur thriller. What more do you want?


	“The End of Oak Street” is preposterous, but it’s also unrespectable fun. It allows the summer movie season to end with a gasp instead of a whimper. On a suburban cul-de-sac in the town of Flowervale, a storybook “normal” family, the Platts — Denise and Greg (Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor) and their two teenagers,  Audrey (Maisy Stella) and Brian (Christian Convery) — wake up one day to discover prehistoric beasts and critters scampering through their neighborhood. At first, they see fast and feathery bird-raptors that look deceptively harmless (watch out: They will eat you). There are stegosauruses wandering through the woods (the woods, by the way, have become a primeval forest). There’s a snake that glides around like the prehistoric world’s largest condom — and yes, there’s a T. Rex, all rapid forward motion and giant jaws, in the tradition of the original 1993 “Jurassic Park” film.
	

	Why is all this happening? We’ll get to the explanation in a moment, but rest assured: It’s entirely ludicrous. Yet “The End of Oak Street,” dumb as it often is, has a distinctive cheeseball flavor that starts with the quirky come-on of the film’s setting. It unfolds in 1982, but there’s no opening title to tell you that. We have to situate ourselves in the period atmosphere, and for a while that’s amusing to do, as we pick up on the songs in the background (“Hit Me With Your Best Shot,” “Turning Japanese”), the drab autumnal furniture, and the size and shape of the homes, which are smaller and brick-uglier than the suburban movie abodes we’re used to. And is that a Gremlin Greg is delivering pizzas in? (Talk about a dinosaur.) Brian and his buddies bike around like refugees from “Stand by Me,” with a tormenting bully in tow. And when the supernatural stuff starts to happen, with nighttime eruptions of glowing white light, it’s right out of a Spielberg movie of the period. (So are Denise and Greg’s marital troubles, which are edging into separation terrain.)

	J.J. Abrams, one of the film’s producers, already cosplayed Spielberg once, in “Super 8.” In “The End of Oak Street,” the writer-director David Robert Mitchell (“It Follows”) nods to the analog Spielberg of the late ’70s and early ’80s, notably in a scene where McGregor’s Greg is running next to a fence. It’s enough to give you a touch of nostalgia for the days when a dinosaur thriller wasn’t all overscaled digital bombast.

	“The End of Oak Street” is sometimes scary, more so than anything in the lumbering last few “Jurassic” sequels. And sometimes it’s a hoot. Intentionally or not? A bit of both, and that’s the film’s knowing but innocent stupido-kitsch dynamic. Denise, Greg, and the kids, along with the teenage neighbor (Jordan Alexa Davis) they come to the aid of (the two girls start flirting, which gives this pulp an au courant edge), don’t have much in the way of weaponry. There are shotguns, which prove less than effective when discharged into a dinosaur’s thick hide, and Brian has a bow and arrow he keeps firing and missing with. (Why not a slingshot?)

	Mostly it’s run, shoot, and hide. But Mitchell stages the creature attacks with witty timing and skill, to the point that when Denise is fending off a T. rex on her porch, you almost believe it. Characters get eaten in a satisfying way, including one shocker I won’t spoil. (There’s also a bizarre moment when two feathery brontosauruses are seen humping against a house; that Denise wants to take a Polaroid of Greg in front of this is beyond nuts.)
	

	The movie finally settles into being the glorified thunder-lizard knockoff it is. The Platts, like the family in the “Quiet Place” films, are in a world of beasts for a reason that makes even less sense the more that you think about it. They’ve passed through a time-warp wormhole, so they’re actually in the prehistoric world — but trapped on a two-mile wide circle of suburbia that’s been preserved. Can they get back? Maybe…by jumping into a shiny glowing globule that appears periodically. It’s not hard to imagine this nonsense having resulted from an executive telling his writer-director, “Figure it the fuck out, or we’ll get AI to script it.”

	David Robert Mitchell was overpraised for “It Follows,” which was like a schlock “elevated” knockoff of “The Hidden,” and he got unfairly lambasted for his artsy but intriguing Lynchian rabbit-hole fantasia “Under the Silver Lake.” That movie put him in movie jail, and “The End of Oak Street” is how you get out of movie jail: by making a dinosaur thriller so blatant in its pandering it proves you’re willing to play the game. Yet Mitchell squeezes bits of B-movie humanity into the crevices, notably in his portrayal of the Platts’ teetering marriage. Hathaway and McGregor overact in tandem in a way that’s vivid and likable. As the film confirms, sometimes a T. rex attack can be the best couples’ therapy. But can we please start the fall movie season now?

title: Paris Jackson Details Keeping Friend Alive After He Overdosed on Her Drugs
description:
Paris Jackson
                          My Friend OD'd on My Drugs ...
body:
Paris Jackson
                          My Friend OD'd on My Drugs ...
                          I Had To Keep Him Alive!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            9:04 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Paris Jackson's diving into the meaning behind one of her new songs ... detailing a traumatic situation she's turned into art after getting sober ... and it involves drugs, an overdose, quick thinking and a happy ending.
      
    
            Michael Jackson's daughter appeared on Alex Cooper's "Call Her Daddy" podcast in an episode published Wednesday ... and she explained her new track "Sirens" is probably her most emotional -- because it's based on her friend overdosing on her drugs.
      
    
            Paris explains she had to keep her pal alive until paramedics arrived ... and they later told her if she hadn't acted as quickly as she did, he would either be brain dead or worse.
      

            She says she had some experience with performing first-aid measures ... but it's still hard to know how she was going to act in the moment -- because fight-or-flight response can make people act in strange ways.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Paris also notes that -- despite the intensity of the moment -- she didn't get sober until more than a year after it all went down ... saying a person can't embrace sobriety until they're truly ready.
      
    
            As for "Sirens" ... Paris says she wrote it in 2021 or 2022 -- and finally took it off the shelf when she realized it fit the vibe of her current album.

title: John Gotti's Grandson Gets Prison Time Shaved Off Amid His Mom's Major Health Issues
description:

                          Catches A Little Break On Prison Time ...
body:
John Gotti's Grandson
                          Catches A Little Break On Prison Time ...
                          As Clock Ticks On Mom's Kidney Donor Search
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            3:50 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 12, 2026
                                8:14 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            John Gotti's grandson Carmine Agnello will have to spend just over a year behind bars as his mom, Victoria Gotti, desperately tries to find a kidney donor during his incarceration, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The federal Bureau of Prisons says Carmine's release date has been pushed up to September 2, 2027, which is a nearly 13-month stretch instead of his original 15-month sentence.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported, Carmine pleaded guilty in 2024 to a $1.1 wire fraud scheme tied to COVID-19 relief funds. Carmine surrendered Monday to the feds and was imprisoned at the Federal Correctional Institution Fairton in Fairton, New Jersey.    
      

            Even though he got some time shaved off, Carmine still faces a major hurdle in trying to supply Victoria with his kidney as her health problems mount while he's in prison.
      
    
            As we told you, Carmine was initially supposed to report to prison on July 20, but the judge gave him an extension so he could donate one of his kidneys to his mom. But Victoria got an infection, and the surgery was shelved.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The judge then gave Carmine until August 10 to donate his kidney and report to prison on September 18. But that didn't work either because Victoria couldn't get medically cleared for the procedure.
      
    
            On Monday, Carmine's attorney, Robert Beltrani, filed court documents asking for a third extension, but the judge turned down the request while postponing Carmine's report time to prison by 2 hours.  
      
    
            Our Gotti sources have told us Carmine only wanted to help Victoria by doing the surgery before going to prison as she battles severe complications from kidney disease. We're also told Carmine was not trying to get out of doing his time behind bars.

title: Rep. Haley Stevens Says Tom Tiffany Is Obsessed With Hunting Wolves
description:

                          Tom Tiffany Only Howls About Wolves ...
body:
Rep. Haley Stevens
                          Tom Tiffany Only Howls About Wolves ...
                          Wisconsin Can Do Better!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            9:27 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Rep. Haley Stevens says Rep. Tom Tiffany has only one thing on his mind as he runs for governor of Wisconsin ... changing hunting laws so he can hunt wolves!!!
      
    
            The Congresswoman from Michigan appeared on CNN Wednesday morning to discuss the Democratic primary for her neighboring state's gubernatorial election in an interview that quickly went off the rails ... when she started howling about Tiffany's alleged wolf hunting obsession.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Rep. Stevens says all of her interactions with Rep. Tiffany, the GOP nominee for Wisconsin governor, have taught her three things ... he's a nice guy, is deeply conservative and his big priority is wolves.
      

            CNN host Pamela Brown didn't hesitate to follow up ... and Rep. Stevens said Rep. Tiffany's talked to her multiple about hunting wolves ... namely, getting laws changed to make it legal.
      
    
            Turns out ... Rep. Tiffany actually co-sponsored a bill in Congress to remove the gray wolf from the federal Endangered Species List and give control over population management to state wildlife agencies.
      
    
            So yes, it seems Rep. Tiffany has wolf hunting on the brain ... though it's unclear if he's as obsessed as Rep. Stevens claims he is.
      
    
            We've reached out to Tiffany's office ... so far word no back.

title: James Haven Reveals Dad Jon Voight's Reaction To Him Coming Out As Gay
description:
James Haven On Jon Voight
                          My Dad Finally Knows Who I Am!!!
body:
James Haven On Jon Voight
                          My Dad Finally Knows Who I Am!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            9:15 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            James Haven's detailing the phone call with his dad, Jon Voight, after he came out as gay ... and it sounds like it was a conversation James was avoiding.
      
    
            The former actor appeared on "All Out With Jon Dean" in an interview published Wednesday morning ... explaining he's often felt somewhat dismissed by his famous father. He says Jon called him multiple times before he finally picked up the phone.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            James says his father told him, "I finally know who you are" ... and they proceeded to have a "really nice chat."
      

            Jon's reaction matches up with what we first reported ... but now James is talking about the conversation on camera for the first time.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The phone call came after we broke they story ... James came out as gay on a live stream with his ex-wife, Romi Imbelli, on her Substack -- reading a letter explaining he didn't have the vocabulary to put how he was feeling into words when he was younger.
      
    
            James said while reading the letter, "I hope my family and others can choose love over fear, understanding over judgment and connection over the beliefs that may have kept us apart.” 
      
    
            It seems his father did just that in his phone call.
